hook.line: Every traveller ends up asking where to plug in, and every phone dies at the worst moment. One verb family covers it.
hook.es: Se me descargó el celular. ¿Dónde puedo cargarlo?
hook.en:
My phone died.
Where can I charge it?

examples.en: Where can I charge my phone?

examples.es: Cargué las cajas en el carro.
examples.en: I loaded the boxes into the car.

examples.es: Cargo el celular en la noche.
examples.en: I charge my phone at night.

rule:
*Cargar* means to load or to charge. *Descargar* is the opposite: to unload, to drain, to download.

*Cargar el celular*: charge your phone.
*Cargar las cajas*: load the boxes.
*Descargar la aplicación*: download the app.
*Descargar el camión*: unload the truck.

When a battery dies on you, use the accidental *se*: *Se me descargó el celular.* The phone is the subject and you are who it happened to.
smallPrint: *La carga* is the load, or the charge. One word family does the work of several English verbs.

yourTurn.prompt: Fill the gap and type the whole sentence: Se me ___ el celular. (descargó / cargó) My phone died.
yourTurn.why: Dying is the opposite of charging, so *descargó*.

yourTurn.prompt: Where can I charge my phone?

yourTurn.why: Getting a file onto your phone is *descargar*.
*Te* says it happened to the person you are talking to.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about us: Se me descargó el celular.
Make the thing plural: Se me descargó el celular.
yourTurn.why: More than one phone, so the verb is *descargaron*.

pitfalls.why: Almost. A battery dying is something that happens to you, so Spanish uses the accidental *se*.
*Cargar* puts something in. Getting an app onto your phone is *descargar*.
The verb matches the phone, and there is only one.

personal: Say what usually dies on you, and when. Try *Se me descarga el celular en la tarde*, or change the thing.
